_note: ThusoIQ's engine API contracts, version one, frozen. The Full Scope's Core acceptance test is "role and scope matrix enforced on every API", and the build plan's Wave 2 writes that matrix down before any engine builds further: every engine's routes live in one file under packages/catalog/apis/, and this file holds what they share — the path convention, the callers, the refusals every route inherits, what may never cross an API, the document sections a route may cite, and the development mock's rules. scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds all thirteen engine files to it, and packages/catalog/apis.lock freezes every route exactly as events.lock freezes events. Nothing here is a running service. The identity service, the Passport P0 and the assistant service answer the routes marked built, in development; everything else is a proposal answered only by packages/mock-api, on loopback, with synthetic data.
_decided: The founder delegated the API conventions to the programme on 14 September 2026 ("propose"). They are decided for this build and are marked as the programme's decision, awaiting a Head of Engineering, who may overturn any of them — by withdrawing and versioning, not by editing a frozen route.

lockHistory.why: apis.lock fingerprints a route's top level and nothing else, so a route's refusals, its callers and the inside of its objects are frozen by the three locks beside it, seeded from the tree at this commit. Every API lock and events.lock is compared with its own history in git from this commit onwards: a line in any commit after it, or in HEAD, that is missing from the next is refused, because a lock line rewritten to match an edited contract is the edit and its cover in one change. History before it was written under no such rule and is not re-read.

conventions.why: One shape for every engine, so a path says whose store it touches before anybody reads the handler. The engine is exactly an engine id from packages/catalog/events.json; the resource is one lower-case hyphenated word; an id is a parameter in braces; an action is one more word, and only after an id — a verb on a collection is a resource of its own (permission-checks, not permissions/check).

passportPaths.why: The Health Passport's paths are named in ThusoIQ Master §26 and the P0 service already answers most of them. They keep their names and are mounted under /v1/record by reference, so the module contract a hospital integrator reads and the path this contract freezes are the same string.

assistantPaths.why: The conversation service answers its own paths: the health and turn routes it runs today, and the versioned /assistant/v1/* family the GilbertOne foundation plan declares for it. They keep their names and are mounted under /assistant by reference, so the address a client calls and the path this contract freezes are the same string, exactly as §26's Passport paths are.

idempotency.why: A charge sent twice is a patient charged twice, and a dispatch sent twice is two nurses driving to one door while another patient waits. Every money write and every dispatch write carries a key the caller chose, and the same key twice is the same act once.

references.why: A field ending Ref points at something an engine stores — a visit, a trip, a payment — and is held to the rule that no route names another engine's resource except through a gateway. A field ending Id names an entry in a contract — a service in services.json, a protocol version in protocols.json, a purpose in consent.json — which every engine may name, because a contract is read by everybody and stored by nobody.

routeShape.why: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE.
The convention above, or a §26 Passport path for the record engine.
The route's version. A changed shape is a new version, never an edit.
What the route does, in a sentence.
Role ids that may call it, from packages/catalog/vetting.json, the grant roles in packages/catalog/consent.json, or the callers below. A route with no callers is a route anybody can call.
Purposes of use from the gate's Purpose union. POPIA section 13 ties processing to a purpose; a route with none cannot be checked against one.
Fields in, each with a type from packages/catalog/feeds.json, whether it is required and why it is there.
Fields out, in the same shape.
At least one {id, status, statement, why}. The route inherits the shared refusals below as well.
Event type@version strings, each live and owned by the route's engine; or an empty list with emitsNoneBecause.
Whether the same call twice is the same act once.
{ section } only when a document gives the route's method and path — which today means the Health Passport's §26 paths and nothing else — or null.

{ section, what } when a document names the capability, message set or state the route serves, with the words in a few; or null. The route that serves it is still the programme's design, and a route with neither is plainly ours.
proposed, or built with evidence naming the handler file and the handler as it is registered there.

True on a POST that changes nothing — a check whose answer is the whole of what it does. Such a route is not a write, so the idempotency rule does not reach it; a route that says it reads and emits an event is refused.
passport-gateway or tool-gateway, when the route reaches another engine's data through one of the two synchronous doors rather than through events.
Required when emits is empty.
Required when status is built: { file, handler }.
As for events: { on, supersededBy, why }, the route keeps its lock line and loses its callers.
For every engine:<id> caller, the live event that engine owns or hears which justifies the call.

[{ field, shownOnce }] for every response field named like a secret in engineRuntime.secretResponseNames. The secret is shown to the caller once, never written to the replay table, and a replay answers with shownOnce in its place.

[{ field, why }] for a request field that is a secret the caller types, such as a cash code. The runtime leaves it out of the digest of the request it keeps for replays, because an unsalted hash of a short code is the code.
{ refusals, tables, why }: the route's own refusals whose recorded writes survive the rollback, and the only tables those writes may touch — an attempt counter and an audit row, never a charge.
Required when built: the mechanism the handler decides callers by, from enforcementMechanisms, and its parameters. The callers are worked out from it.
missing, when the handler does not yet enforce the intended callers; the build fails on it.
Required with enforcement: missing — what the handler does today.

callers.name: Nobody signed in
callers.why: Starting a sign-in and reading a public contract are the only things somebody with no session may do.

callers.name: A patient, in their own session
callers.why: The person a record, a booking or a payment is about. Not a vetting role, because a patient is not vetted.

callers.name: The person the resource is about
callers.why: A nurse reading her own vetting standing, or anybody reading their own account. The subject token of the session must be the subject of the resource.

callers.name: Thuso Line desk agent
callers.why: Books and supports by phone, WhatsApp and USSD on a patient's behalf, and is recorded as the actor rather than the patient.

callers.name: Care dispatcher
callers.why: Matches visits to nurses when the automatic offer has not been accepted.

callers.name: Operations and safety desk
callers.why: Receives panic, overdue check-ins and SOS, and holds escalation authority on the rota.

callers.name: Medical Director
callers.why: The only role that ratifies a clinical protocol.

callers.name: Thuso Ride responder
callers.why: Transport, not medical care. Sees the emergency summary during a trip through the responder-on-trip grant and nothing else.

callers.name: Partner facility admissions desk
callers.why: Accepts, wait-lists or declines an admission request and opens a pre-arrival packet through a share link.

callers.name: Somebody on the machine itself
callers.why: The identity service answers its /health/ routes only to a caller on the loopback address. That is a place, not a role, and the contract says so rather than pretending an operator is checked.

callers.name: The party who reported an incident
callers.why: Containing an incident is the reviewer's work or the reporter's own follow-through, and nobody else's.

callers.name: A developer holding a development token
callers.why: Minting synthetic subjects in the Passport P0 is development-only, behind the development flag and a developer token, and never a patient or a clinician action.

callers.name: The founder, signed in to founder access
callers.why: Founder access (packages/catalog/founder-access.json) lets one person — the founder, holding a password and an authenticator — sign in to the assistant service and reveal its two Azure keys. It is not a vetting role and not an operator: nobody else can hold it, it is dark until switched on by hand on the box, and it reaches nothing but its own founder routes — the four of 24 September 2026 and, since 28 September, the eight that keep the assistant's settings history and the provider key vault (packages/catalog/founder-access.json#ownership).

engineCallers.why: An engine calls another engine's route over mutual TLS because something happened that it owns or hears. A bare engine caller let any engine call clinical triage, next-of-kin alerts or a claim; each engine caller now names one engine and the live event, which that engine owns or subscribes to, that justifies the call.

supplierCallers.why: Payment results arrive on the payment-result door.
Payout advice arrives on the payout-advice door.
Delivery receipts arrive on the message-delivery door.
Inbound WhatsApp is a door to add, not a route.
USSD sessions are a door to add, not a route.
Identity verification results belong on a door; the identity service's existing callback is the one legacy exception, and it says so.
Criminal-record clearance results are a door to add.
Lab results arrive on a door to add.
HL7 v2 ADT and discharge messages arrive on a door to add.
Ambulance dispatch acknowledgements arrive on the emergency-acknowledgement door.
Device and wearable readings from a vendor cloud arrive on a door to add.
Speech transcripts arrive on the speech-transcript door.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: Nothing: the handler for this route calls none of signedIn, asParty, asOperator, tokenFor or requesterOf, and resolves no session cookie.
enforcementMechanisms.why: The handler asks for nothing, and must not quietly ask for a session.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: signedIn(req, res), or the session cookie resolved directly, in the handler for this route, and no vetting guard.
enforcementMechanisms.why: A signed-in person acting on their own account: the session cookie resolved to a person, through signedIn() or directly.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: asParty(req, res) in the handler for this route, and no operator guard, gate decision, vault decision or read of the caller's own standing.
enforcementMechanisms.why: Anybody on the vetting register, cleared or not.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: asParty(req, res) and a read of the caller's own standing, vetting!.standing(held.actor.party.id), with nothing in the handler naming another party.
enforcementMechanisms.why: A vetted party reading their own standing.

enforcementMechanisms.callers: the vetting roles granted the named capability
enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: The capability the operator guard asOperator checks in its own body; or a gate.access call's capability when the call cannot admit the subject; or the vault's capability when the vault method refuses a party acting on itself or asks the gate only for administrative operations.
enforcementMechanisms.why: The gate or the vault decides against a capability, which packages/catalog/vetting.json grants to roles.

enforcementMechanisms.callers: the roles granted the capability, and self
enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: A gate call or vault method that does not refuse a party acting on itself and asks the gate, with a purpose that becomes subject access on the caller's own record, for an operation the gate's SELF_OPERATIONS lets a subject perform by identity.
enforcementMechanisms.why: A reviewer, or the party the evidence is about acting on their own file.

enforcementMechanisms.callers: the roles granted the capability, and incident-reporter
enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: A comparison of the incident's reporter with the caller and a grants check for the capability, with the operator guard's capability matching it where the handler calls the guard.
enforcementMechanisms.why: The reviewer holding the capability in good standing, or the party who reported this incident.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: The route's path lies under the prefix the server refuses to anybody not on the loopback address, and the handler asks for no session or party.
enforcementMechanisms.why: Answered only to a caller on the machine itself.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: tokenFor(req, 'Patient') in the statement that answers this method and path.

enforcementMechanisms.callers: patient when patientToo, and the grant roles whose gateway block reads one of grantReads, or writes when grantWrites
enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: requesterOf(req) and the gateway method the statement calls. The roles it admits are worked out from the reads values that method and #hold refuse, whether it requires a writable grant, and the category a grant's scope must name, and they must equal the roles grantReads, grantWrites and patientToo describe.
enforcementMechanisms.why: The gateway validates a grant artefact for its role on every call, from the role's gateway block in packages/catalog/consent.json.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: tokenFor(req, 'Operator') in the statement that answers this method and path.
enforcementMechanisms.why: Who breaks the glass comes from an operator credential, never the request body.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: One of the acceptor calls listed here, in the handler for this route. The supplier is that acceptor's, and it must be the supplier enforcedBy names.
enforcementMechanisms.why: The legacy identity-provider callback, and nothing else.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: tokenFor(req, 'Developer') in the statement that answers this method and path.
enforcementMechanisms.why: Development-only minting behind the development flag and a developer credential minted at the console (packages/catalog/passport-gateway.json, developerCredential).

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: The module the evidence file exports as engine is the route's own engine and registers exactly this route's key with a handler.
enforcementMechanisms.callers: the route's engine callers and named roles, which the runtime binder admits from this contract; never self, anonymous, loopback, a supplier or a developer, which the binder cannot tell apart from anybody
enforcementMechanisms.why: A route built on packages/engines is admitted by the binder, which reads its callers from this contract before the handler runs; the handler never decides who called it. In development the role arrives in a header and is believed.

enforcementMechanisms.callers: every grant role in packages/catalog/consent.json that does not read aggregates, as the grant the link rides on names
enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: tokenFor(req, 'Link') in the statement that answers this method and path.
enforcementMechanisms.why: A share link is opened by whoever holds its secret, acting as the recipient of the grant it rides on (Record P1, Wave 4). The secret comes off the Authorization header and nowhere else, and a link is never made for a role that reads aggregates, so the callers are exactly the identifiable grant roles.

enforcementMechanisms.callers: the route's own declared engine callers, and nothing else
enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: The statement that answers this method and path calls neither tokenFor nor requesterOf, so it asks for no patient session, grant, share-link secret or development credential at all, and every caller the route declares is an engine:* name.
enforcementMechanisms.why: There is no OIDC or mutual TLS between services yet (§22), so a machine caller is today distinguished from anybody else on the loopback only by the loopback itself (Wave 6, GET /v1/record/encounter-statuses/{encounterRef}@1). Used only for a route that trades no clinical content either way, so a caller nobody can yet authenticate costs nothing sensitive.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: founder.signIn( in the assistant service's handler for this route, after founder.gate(req.headers), and no other session, party or credential check.
enforcementMechanisms.why: The founder's password and authenticator code, checked together by apps/assistant-api/src/lib/founder-access.ts, behind the founder-access switch.

enforcementMechanisms.extractedFrom: founder.sessionFrom(req.headers.cookie) in the assistant service's handler for this route, after founder.gate(req.headers), and no other session, party or credential check.
enforcementMechanisms.why: A live founder session cookie, minted by a founder sign-in and held in the assistant service's memory only.

_enforcementNote: A built route's callers are not written, they are worked out: from the capability in packages/catalog/vetting.json, the grant roles' gateway blocks in packages/catalog/consent.json, or the credential roles in packages/catalog/passport-gateway.json, as the route's enforcedBy says its handler decides — and the check requires the contract's callers to equal that list and finds the mechanism in the handler. The third review found twelve built routes naming callers their handlers did not enforce. Where a handler enforces nothing today, the contract keeps the intended callers, says enforcement: missing with the finding, and the build fails until the handler enforces them.
_contractIdsNote: A field ending Id names either an entry in a contract, listed here with the contract it points at, or an identifier the route's own engine issues, listed in that engine file's ownIds. Anything else — patientId, visitId — is another engine's resource under a name that dodged the reference rule, and is refused; it must be an opaque Ref.

documentQuotes.why: A capabilityNamed quote is the document's own words, found in the cited section once both are lower-cased and their punctuation set aside; or it says paraphrase: true. The documents are untracked, so the check converts them with textutil when they are present, and holds the quotes to quoteVerification when they are not.

quoteVerification.why: The documents are untracked and confidential, so most checkouts cannot compare a quote with them. This records when the quotes were last compared, against which version of each document and over which quotes, so a quote can only change on a machine that can check it: without the documents the build fails if the quotes no longer hash to this, and with them it fails unless this describes what it has just verified.

sharedRefusals.statement: This route does not take calls from your role.
sharedRefusals.why: The role and scope matrix is enforced on every route, and the refusal says which half refused rather than failing silently.

sharedRefusals.statement: This route does not serve the purpose you gave.
sharedRefusals.why: A read made for billing that reaches a diagnosis is the processing POPIA section 13 forbids, and it is refused before anything is opened.

sharedRefusals.statement: A field this route needs was not sent.
sharedRefusals.why: A route that guesses a missing field has invented part of somebody's request.

sharedRefusals.statement: A money or dispatch write needs an idempotency key.
sharedRefusals.why: Without one, a retry on a bad connection is a second charge or a second nurse.

sharedRefusals.statement: That address could not be read.
sharedRefusals.why: A path that does not decode is refused in words, rather than thrown at the process that was answering it.

sharedRefusals.statement: That idempotency key was already used for a different request.
sharedRefusals.why: The same key twice is the same act once. A key sent again with a different amount or a different visit is not a retry, and answering it with the first result would tell the caller something happened that did not.

sharedRefusals.statement: This address is answered at more than one version. Name the version you are calling.
sharedRefusals.why: Answering whichever version was declared first would hand a caller who meant another a different shape and different refusals, and nothing would say so. POST /v1/money/payments is live at versions one and two, and until this refusal version two could not be reached by its address at all.

sharedRefusals.statement: This address is not declared at the version you named.
sharedRefusals.why: A version nobody declared has no callers, no purpose and no refusals to hold a call to, so it is refused rather than answered as the nearest one.

trustNames.why: A trust-named field that is a number is the Trust Score renamed, and no route anywhere carries one. Outside Verify's own routes a trust-named field is the badge tier or nothing; inside them a person reading their own vetting standing is reading about themselves, which is what those routes are for. The event contract's trust words include standing; this list does not, because the identity service's consent routes already answer with a consent's standing — whether a purpose was agreed to — which is not about anybody's trust, and a word list that refuses a built route for sharing a word has stopped being about the Trust Score.

neverCrossesAnApi.why: The event contract already refuses these on the bus. The same refusal holds for every request and response: no identity number, no transcript, no card or bank number, no Trust Score under any name, no numeric trust-named field and no trust-named field outside Verify but the badge tier, and no field named for a sealed category. Names, phone numbers and email addresses are not in this list — the identity service takes them, and it is the one place that may.

objectFields.why: packages/catalog/feeds.json has no object type, and this contract extends nothing there. A field whose value is a JSON object keeps the nearest type — string for one object, list for a list of them — and says "object": true, so the generated clients type it as an object rather than lying that it is text, and the mock answers it with an empty object rather than a string.

innerShapes.fields: An object field's inside, as a list of fields in the same shape as a route's own — field, type, required, why, and object with fields of its own — to any depth.
innerShapes.nullable: true when the value may be null rather than absent. A field that is always sent and sometimes null is required and nullable; a field that is sometimes left out is not required.
innerShapes.shapeFrom: packages/catalog/<file>.json#<dotted path>, in place of fields, for an object whose inside a contract already decides: a setting's limits are keys packages/catalog/settings.json#setting gives, and a setting's value is whichever kind its type gives in #types. The section is hashed with its commentary left out, so a change there is a change to every route that takes its shape from it.
innerShapes.why: A settings migration changed a live route's inner rows under an unchanged fingerprint, because the inside of an object was described in its why and apis.lock hashes only the top level. A shape written as a sentence cannot be frozen, compared or checked against what a handler returns. So every object a route carries declares its inside as data, packages/catalog/apis.shapes.lock freezes it, and the routes that predate the rule are listed in proseOnlyObjects.

proseOnlyObjects.why: These route versions were frozen before an object's inside had to be declared, and their objects are described only in prose. A frozen route cannot honestly be given a shape nobody has checked against its handler, so each is listed by exact version rather than guessed at. The list only shrinks: a route leaves it by declaring its inner shapes, which appends its line to packages/catalog/apis.shapes.lock, and the build refuses an entry the sealed prose-only lines there do not already name. A new route, or a new version of one of these, declares its shapes from the start.

legacyCallbacks.why: A supplier never calls a route. The identity service already answers one supplier callback — POST /vetting/identity/callback, the identity provider's result — which predates the doors. It is mapped here because it is built, marked legacyCallback with the door it should become, and refused everywhere else: no route may be a supplier callback unless it is built, marked, and names a door to add in its own engine file.

clinicalContent._alwaysNote: The gateway exception is for engines whose work is care. Money, Core and Movement never carry clinical content, through the gateway or otherwise: a claim's coding carried to Money through the gateway was the gateway switching the rule off for the one engine that faces payers. A list of reason codes is clinical content too, because it names the discriminators that fired; a single reason code for a cancellation names no condition.
clinicalContent.why: No engine holds a copy of a record. A route in any engine but record that carries clinical content — a reading, a finding, a dose, a clinical record by name — must declare that it goes through the Passport's consent gateway; otherwise it carries a reference to the entry, and the entry stays where the grant decides who reads it.

gateways.why: The one synchronous door to clinical data: consent, purpose and scope checked and logged on every call.
GilbertOne's allow-listed tool calls (§15D). A tool reaches another engine's action only by name from the allow-list, never a generic call.

_documentSectionsNote: The sections the build plan's ◆ marks rest on: the ThusoIQ Master's §5, §8–§15D, §26 and §36, and the Full Scope's Core and engine tables. The documents are not in the repository, so this list is the copy the check holds routes to; a section added here should be one somebody can open.

mock._versionHeaderNote: A method and path can be live at more than one version, as POST /v1/money/payments is, and the path does not say which. The caller names the version in this header. Where a path is live at one version the header may be left out; where it is live at more, leaving it out is refused with route-version-required, and a version the path is not declared at is refused with route-version-not-declared. The mock and the engine runtime's door read the same rule from packages/mock-api/src/mock.ts.
mock.why: Screens are built against the contract before any engine exists, so the mock answers every route from fixtures derived from this contract and refuses exactly as the route declares: the wrong role, the wrong purpose, a missing field, a missing idempotency key, and — when a test asks for it by id — each of the route's own refusals with its status and its sentence. It binds to loopback, refuses to start without the flag, and nothing in deploy/ may name it.

engineRuntime._binderCannotAdmitNote: Callers that are a relationship or a place rather than a role: self is the subject of the resource, incident-reporter the party who opened one incident, loopback a socket address, anonymous nobody, developer a credential minted at a console. A header naming one proves none of them, so the binder refuses all five and a route that needs one needs a handler that checks.
engineRuntime._secretResponseNamesNote: A response field whose name ends in one of these is a secret shown once. Its route lists it in secretResponseFields with the sentence a replay answers with in its place, and the runtime never writes it to the replay table. The list is the build's, so a new secret-shaped name is added here rather than slipping past; a field is matched by the end of its name, so stateCode and feeCode are not secrets and cashCode is.

refusals.statement: A field this route needs was sent in the wrong shape.
refusals.why: A route that reads a word where it declared a number has guessed what the caller meant.

refusals.statement: The engine could not answer that request, and nothing it started was kept.
refusals.why: A handler that failed half-way is rolled back and its events dropped, so a fault is never half an act.

refusals.statement: No route in the contract answers that method and path.
refusals.why: The runtime answers the contract and nothing beside it.

refusals.statement: Only an engine declared in the event contract is bound, and only once.
refusals.why: An engine nobody declared owns nothing, and one bound twice is two answers to every route.

refusals.statement: A handler is registered only for a route the contract declares.
refusals.why: A handler with no route in the contract is a door nobody reviewed, with no callers, no purpose and no refusals.

refusals.statement: A withdrawn route is not answered.
refusals.why: Its correction is the next version, and a handler for the old one keeps the defect running.

refusals.statement: An engine answers only its own routes.
refusals.why: An engine answering another's route is writing to a resource whose store it does not own.

refusals.statement: An engine does its own next step in its own code, not through its own route.
refusals.why: An engine calling itself through the binder is a loop with one member and no owner, as a subscription to itself would be.

refusals.statement: An engine hears only the events that list it as a subscriber.
refusals.why: Every subscriber is declared in the frozen contract, so a new consequence of an event is a reviewed change and not a line of code.

refusals.statement: An idempotent write needs to know who is asking.
refusals.why: A stored answer is handed back only to the caller who asked for it. A person the binder cannot tell apart from another would be handed whichever answer was stored first under their key.

refusals.statement: An engine's store runs one statement at a time on its own tables: it attaches nothing, ends no transaction, and neither copies nor reconfigures the file.
refusals.why: Another engine's store is reached through a route or an event, never a file, and the binder's transaction is what lets a refusal or a fault undo everything a handler started.

refusals.statement: The runtime's own tables in an engine's store are not the engine's to read or change.
refusals.why: The replay table is the binder's record of what it has already answered. An engine that edits it can make a second charge look like a replay, or a first one look like it never happened.

refusals.statement: A refusal keeps only the writes its route declares: one insert or update into a table named in keptOnRefusal, made by a route handler, for a refusal named there.
refusals.why: Everything else a refused handler did is rolled back. A way to keep an attempt counter and an audit row must not become a way to keep a charge.

engineRuntime.why: The engines are built one route at a time on a development runtime: a handler bound to a route in this contract, run against its own engine's SQLite store, publishing to an in-process bus held to packages/catalog/events.json. The binder admits a route's callers from this contract and refuses the rest; a route with no handler is answered by the mock. It refuses to start without the flag, binds to loopback, believes a caller's role from a development header, and nothing in deploy/ may name it.

refusals.statement: Every route names the roles that may call it and the purposes it serves.
refusals.why: The Full Scope's Core acceptance test is a role and scope matrix enforced on every API. A route that names neither has no matrix to enforce.

refusals.statement: Every route declares at least one refusal of its own, with a status, a sentence and the reason.
refusals.why: The valuable part of a route is what it will not do. A route that only says yes is a route whose no is invented at three in the morning by whoever is on call.

refusals.statement: Every route names the events it emits, each live and owned by its own engine, or says why it emits none.
refusals.why: Cross-engine work travels as events. A route that changes something and tells nobody is a direct call waiting to be written.

refusals.statement: No route names another engine's resource in its path or its fields, except through the Passport gateway or GilbertOne's tool gateway.
refusals.why: An engine that reads another's store is two engines that must be deployed, secured and changed together. The two synchronous doors are the only exceptions, and each checks who is asking and why.

refusals.statement: Clinical content crosses an API only through the Passport gateway. Everywhere else a route carries a reference to the entry.
refusals.why: No engine holds a copy of a record. A reading in a devices payload that is not going through the gateway is a second copy with none of the record's protections.

refusals.statement: Every money write and every dispatch write is idempotent and requires an idempotency key.
refusals.why: A retry on a dropped connection must not charge twice or send two nurses.

refusals.statement: A supplier never calls a route. It calls a door in packages/catalog/feeds.json, which answers no until its switch-on conditions are evidenced.
refusals.why: A supplier callback added as a route skips every condition a door holds: the contract, the credential, the named operator and the refused fields.

refusals.statement: No request or response carries an identity number, a transcript, a card or bank number, a Trust Score under any name, a trust-named field other than the badge tier, or a field named for a sealed category.
refusals.why: Every one of these is refused on the bus already, and an API is a wider audience than the bus: it reaches phones, browsers and partners.

refusals.statement: A route marked built names the file and the handler that answers it, and the check finds that handler there.
refusals.why: A contract that says built about something nobody wrote is the readiness overstatement this repository exists to refuse.

refusals.statement: A route says a document names its endpoint only when the document gives the method and the path, and says a document names its capability only by citing the section and the words.
refusals.why: "The documents say so" is only evidence when a reader can open the section and find it there. Only §26 names endpoints; elsewhere the documents name what an engine does, and counting the route that does it as named in the documents overstates how much of the design is theirs.

refusals.statement: While the API contract is frozen, no route in apis.lock may disappear or change shape. A new version is a new entry, and a wrong one is withdrawn, not edited.
refusals.why: A screen built against version one is still in somebody's pocket. Editing version one in place breaks it without a word.

refusals.statement: The API contract is frozen, and the build refuses a contract that says it is not.
refusals.why: Every lock check sits behind the flag; a boolean that switches them off is a door any change walks through.

refusals.statement: The development mock answers only on loopback, addressed to a loopback name, only with the development flag set — checked by the library as well as the server — and only with synthetic data, and nothing that deploys may name it.
refusals.why: A mock that answers every route with a yes, reachable from outside, is a fake health service with a real address. A page that rebinds its own hostname to 127.0.0.1 arrives from loopback, so the address alone lets it in, and a library that can be imported without the flag skips the door the server goes through.

refusals.statement: A built route's callers are exactly those its handler enforces, worked out from the mechanism it names, and a handler that enforces nothing yet fails the build.
refusals.why: The contract said admin-only routes were an operator's and the Passport's were narrower than the gateway allowed. A caller list that is written rather than worked out is a claim about security nobody tested.

refusals.statement: No route takes calls from any engine. Each engine caller is one engine, justified by a live event it owns or hears.
refusals.why: Mutual TLS proves which engine is calling. It does not make every engine entitled to call clinical triage or a next-of-kin alert.

refusals.statement: A field ending Id is an entry in a named contract or an identifier the route's own engine issues. Anything else is a Ref.
refusals.why: A reference to another engine's store under a name ending Id walked round the rule that only a gateway reaches another engine's data.

refusals.statement: A capability quote is found word for word in the section it cites, or it says it is a paraphrase.
refusals.why: Forty phrases that read like quotes were not in the documents as written, which is the same overstatement as counting a route as named when only its capability was.

refusals.statement: A frozen route's refusals are frozen with it: each id, its status and its sentence, and every engine refusal whose answeredBy names it. Adding, removing or rewording one is a new version of the route, never an edit.
refusals.why: A screen shows the sentence a route answered with, and a caller branches on the id. A settings migration reworded refusals on a live route under a fingerprint that never looked at them, and only a person reading the diff saw it.

refusals.statement: A refusal routes share keeps its status and its sentence for as long as it is declared, and different words are a different id. A shared settings refusal changes only with a new version of the settings route shape.
refusals.why: A shared sentence changed in place changes the answer of every route that inherits it at once, and no caller can stay on the old one. A version on the shared list would only be a label on that edit.

refusals.statement: An engine refusal is answered only by the routes its answeredBy names, and the engine runtime refuses it from any other.
refusals.why: A refusal declared for the whole engine and answered by a frozen route is a refusal added to that route without its version changing, which is how encounter-signature-unconfirmed reached two frozen Care routes.

refusals.statement: A frozen route never takes calls from a caller, for a purpose or on an engine's justification it was not frozen with. A narrowing is recorded as a line of its own; a widening is a new version.
refusals.why: A caller added to a frozen route widens who reaches it without anybody deciding to version it, which is how GET /v1/care/settings@1 gained the doctor. And a caller removed for a reason must not drift back, so the narrowest recorded line is the one in force.

refusals.statement: Every object a route carries declares its inside as fields, or names the contract section that decides it. Only the route versions in proseOnlyObjects are excused, and that list only shrinks.
refusals.why: A shape written as a sentence cannot be frozen, compared or checked against what a handler returns, and a settings migration changed one on a live route without anything noticing.

refusals.statement: No line in a lock file is ever edited or removed. History is added to.
refusals.why: A lock line rewritten to match an edited contract is the edit and its cover in one change, and the check comparing the two passes.
